title: Create an Instagram Comment-to-DM Automation
html:
Imagine every time someone drops a comment on your Instagram post, they get an instant, friendly DM from you, without you even touching your phone. That’s Comment-to-DM Automation.

It’s like having a superpower where every comment turns into a private conversation, automatically. No more missed opportunities. No more forgetting to reply. Just smooth, real-time engagement that feels personal, not robotic.

Whether it’s a giveaway, a product inquiry, or a casual question, AP3K slides into your follower’s DMs for you, starting conversations while you’re busy running your brand (or, let’s be real, binge-watching your favorite series).

Once your Instagram account is connected to AP3K, you’re ready to create your first automation. Here’s exactly how to do it in just a few clicks:

Before you begin

  • An Instagram account connected to AP3K
  • A published post or reel for the automation to watch
  • The DM you want to send: text, or an image with buttons

Step 1: Go to the Dashboard

After logging in, you’ll land on the AP3K dashboard. This is your main control panel.

Step 2: Open Automations

Open Automations in the sidebar to see your saved automations. Above the list, All / Basic / Flow filter what you are looking at.

Step 3: Create a Post Automation

Click + New automation. The dialog offers three quick automations:

  • Post automation: replies when someone comments on a post or reel
  • Story automation: replies to story replies and reactions
  • Chat automation: replies to keywords sent in DMs

Below those sit the advanced options — Flow builder and AI assisted flow builder — plus a conversation starter and ready-made templates.

Choose Post automation for a comment-to-DM flow.

Step 4: Configure Your Automation

You’ll now walk through a few quick setup steps:

  1. Select Post or Reel: choose a specific post or reel and click its thumbnail, or choose Any post for an account-wide campaign.
  2. Set Trigger: choose Any comment or a specific word (s). Add campaign keywords such as LINK, GUIDE or INFO; choose Contains keyword or Exact match.
  3. Set Public comment reply: write saved replies in Manual, or use an AI prompt. Free accounts can generate a prompt and preview samples within the preview allowance; publishing AI replies requires a paid plan.
  4. Choose Message format: plain text, text with button (up to three links), image with button, or attachment.
  5. Add optional steps: an Opener message can ask the person to tap before the final DM. Paid plans can add Collect info, Ask to follow and Follow up message.

Use the live preview to review the reply, DM and button labels. This automation listens for new matching interactions after publication. To process eligible comments from the previous seven days, review and run the separate Backtrack comments action.

Step 5: Publish and Go Live

Choose Publish to open the safety review. Read its findings, adjust the setup if needed, then confirm publication. Verify Enabled status and test a fresh interaction from another account.

Pro Tip

Always test your automation by commenting from another account to make sure it’s firing correctly.

You should now have

A live post automation that watches the post you chose, replies to matching comments, and sends your DM, running whether or not you’re online.

Next: Triggers in automation

Real-World Cases and Examples

  • Giveaway Madness: “Comment ‘Done’ to enter!” → Auto DM bonus entry steps and watch excitement build.
  • Flash Sales: “Comment ‘SALE’ for your code!” → DM them a time-limited discount and drive FOMO.
  • Product Teasers: “Want early access? Comment ‘VIP’!” → DM secret launch info to your biggest fans.
  • Service Bookings: “Need help? Comment ‘Consult’!” → DM your booking link and get those calls lined up.
  • Event Hype: “Coming to our event? Comment ‘RSVP’!” → DM them venue details and save the date.
  • Freebies & Guides: “Want the checklist? Comment ‘Guide’!” → DM them the PDF instantly.
  • Support Made Easy: “Got an issue? Comment ‘Help’!” → DM a quick troubleshooting guide.
  • Newsletter Signups: “Stay updated! Comment ‘Subscribe’!” → DM signup link.
  • Lead Magnets: “Grab the resource! Comment ‘Download’!” → DM a freebie and collect leads.

Best Ways to Set Up

  • Mix up your replies. Random message variations = natural convo vibes.
  • Always drop a clear CTA: “Tap the link!”, “Reply YES!”, “Claim now!”
  • Keep it on-brand: Sound like you, not a bot. Emojis? Humor? Go for it.
  • Always preview/test with a dummy account first. Nobody likes broken automations.
  • If expecting loads of comments (think big promos), let AI Auto-Reply help you out without missing a beat.
description: Imagine every time someone drops a comment on your Instagram post, they get an instant, friendly DM from you, without you even touching your phone. That’s Comment-to-DM Automation.

title: Choose Which Post or Reel an Automation Watches
html:
Post is the first card in the automation editor, and it answers one question: which piece of content is this automation listening to?

Nothing else runs until this is set. A trigger with no post attached has nothing to watch.

Choose the post scope

Open the dropdown on the Post card:

  • a specific post or reel — pick one piece of published content from the grid. The automation listens on that post.
  • Any post — listen across the account’s posts and reels. Use a relevant campaign keyword so unrelated comments do not receive the wrong link.

Pick a specific post and a grid of your published content appears underneath. Click a thumbnail to select it and review the selected post in the preview. Use the search field or Refresh if the post you need is missing.

To prepare a campaign for your next upload, use the Auto-DM on next post or reel template. The quick Post picker itself has the two choices above.

Which one to use

A specific post is the right default. Most automations exist for one campaign — a giveaway, a launch, a lead magnet — and the DM you write only makes sense next to that post.

Any post suits a broad, evergreen campaign. Check that the message makes sense across your feed, including future posts.

Avoid overlapping campaigns

Review other active automations before publishing. Give campaigns distinct keywords or use the Flow builder to route people through one conversation. Multiple keywords in a quick automation are alternatives that lead to the same response.

Changing the post later

The selection is not locked once you publish. Reopen the automation, click the Post card, and choose different content — the trigger, replies and DM all stay as they were. This is the quick way to reuse a campaign that worked: point last month’s automation at this month’s post rather than rebuilding it.

Reels, image posts and carousels all work the same way. Stories do not appear here — those belong to a story automation, which is a separate type.

title: Instagram Automation Triggers
html:
Triggers tell AP3K when to jump into action: a comment on a post, an interaction with a story, or a message sent to your inbox. Choose the automation type first, then set a rule that matches your call to action.

1: Any comment

If you want to keep it simple and respond to any eligible comment on your selected post or reel, choose Any comment. This is useful for giveaways where the caption says “comment anything to enter.”

Someone comments “Love this 🥰” on your product reel → AP3K can send your thank-you message and offer link.

2: Specific keywords

Choose a specific word (s) when the campaign asks people to comment LINK, GUIDE, INFO or another word. Type a keyword into Add keyword and press Enter. Each becomes a chip you can remove with its ×. Matching any one of the saved keywords is enough.

Contains keyword matches the word or phrase inside a longer comment. Exact match requires the comment to match the keyword. Matching ignores letter case. For example, “What’s the price?” can match price in Contains mode; price does not match pricing.

AP3K does not offer an Intent Match trigger in this editor. Add the different words your audience uses, or choose Any comment when every comment should qualify.

When to use which

You want to…Use
DM people who comment on the selected postAny comment
DM people using a campaign word in a sentenceSpecific keywords + Contains keyword
Require the campaign word aloneSpecific keywords + Exact match

Also trigger on shares

This switch runs the automation when someone shares the selected post to your DMs. It does not mean sharing the post to any other inbox. AP3K checks the shared post against the configured post scope.

One DM per user

Even if someone comments several times, they get only one initial DM from this automation. The same conversation can still continue through its buttons and configured steps. Turn this on for campaigns where people tend to comment repeatedly.

Stories and incoming DMs

A Story automation selects Mentions me, Reacts or Replies. A Chat automation selects specific keywords or Any incoming DM. These are separate from the Post automation’s comment trigger.

Best practices for triggers

  • Use a short, clear word in both the caption and your automation.
  • Test a matching comment and a non-matching comment from another account.
  • Check which other automations listen to the same posts or inbox.
  • Keep the reply relevant to the promise people responded to.

title: Public Comment Replies You Write Yourself
html:
When your automation fires, it does two things: it sends the DM, and — if you let it — it leaves a public reply under the comment that triggered it.

The public reply is the part everyone else scrolling the post can see. It tells the commenter to go and check their inbox, and it tells everyone else that commenting gets a response.

Turning it on

The Public comment reply card has a toggle on its right. Off, the automation still sends DMs — it just stays out of your comment section.

Switch it on and choose Manual to write the replies yourself. (The other tab, AI, generates a fresh reply for every comment from a prompt.)

Writing the replies

Type a reply and press Enter. It joins the list above the field, with a bin icon to delete it. Add up to 20 saved replies.

Insert {{username}} to drop the commenter’s Instagram handle into the reply — there’s a shortcut button on the right of the input. “Sent it over, {{username}} 💌” reads like you typed it; “Sent it over” repeated forty times does not.

Add three or more

Three or more short replies make a busy comment section less repetitive. AP3K can rotate the saved replies rather than posting the same sentence every time.

With more than one reply saved, Rotate randomly per comment selects from your saved replies, so the section reads like a person answering rather than a script.

Three or four short variants is plenty:

  • “Just sent it 📩”
  • “Check your DMs, {{username}}!”
  • “On its way — have a look at your message requests too”
  • “Sent! Let me know if it doesn’t land”

Limit how many go out

The public reply limit offers no cap, 100 or 200 replies per post. Choose a limit deliberately. Once the cap is reached, public replies stop while eligible DM delivery can continue.

This matters on a post that takes off. A hundred replies from your account under one post is engagement; a thousand is a wall of your own name, and Instagram’s spam systems notice. If you want the reasoning and the numbers, see Limit public replies.

Pro Tip

Mention the message request folder in at least one variant. First-time DMs from an account someone doesn’t follow often land there, and “check your requests” is the difference between a delivered DM and an unread one.

title: AI Public Comment Replies
html:
Writing four public replies by hand is fine. Writing enough of them that a busy post never repeats itself is not — which is where the AI tab comes in.

Instead of a list of replies, you give AP3K a prompt. Every comment that fires the automation gets its own reply, written on the spot from that prompt and the comment it’s answering.

Setting it up

In the Public comment reply card, switch the toggle on and pick AI — it’s the recommended tab.

Writing the prompt

The prompt is a description of what the reply should do and how it should sound, not the reply itself. The default is a good shape to copy:

Thank {{username}} for commenting and let them know a special link is waiting in their DMs, with a friendly, cheerful tone.

Three things make a prompt work:

  • The job. Point them to their DMs, thank them, answer the question — say which.
  • The tone. “Friendly and cheerful”, “short and dry”, “warm, no emojis”. The AI will otherwise default to a brightness that may not be yours.
  • {{username}} where you want the commenter’s handle.

You have 400 characters, and the counter under the box tracks them.

Regenerate prompt rewrites the prompt itself — useful when you know roughly what you want but not how to phrase it. Show preview renders sample replies so you can hear the tone before anyone else does.

AI or manual?

Use AI when comment volume is high or unpredictable, when comments are actual questions rather than a keyword, or when you want the section to look genuinely conversational.

Use manual when the reply must be exact — a legal phrase, a promo code, a specific instruction — or when you’d rather approve every sentence your account posts in public.

Preview before publishing

The AI writes in public, under your name, at comment speed. Run Show preview and read a few samples first — a prompt that’s slightly off produces dozens of slightly-off replies before you notice.

The per-post cap in the card header applies here exactly as it does to manual replies: once it’s reached, public replies stop and DMs carry on.

Free previews and paid publishing

Free users can generate a prompt and sample replies within the preview allowance. This lets you review the tone before upgrading. When a Free account attempts to publish an automation with AI replies, AP3K shows AI only available on paid plans.

Choose Manual and review your saved replies if you want to publish without AI, or move to a paid plan. Published AI replies also depend on your plan’s AI allowance and the connected provider being available.

title: DM Message Layouts: Plain Text, Buttons and Attachments
html:
The Message card is the DM itself. The dropdown in its header decides what shape that DM takes — and the shape matters more than most people expect, because a tappable button gets clicked far more often than a link pasted into a sentence.

Plain text

Just words. Up to 1,000 characters, links included.

Instagram turns a pasted URL into a tappable link, so plain text is perfectly workable for a single link — it just looks like a normal message rather than a card. Use it for conversational openers, answers to questions, and anywhere a designed card would feel like an ad.

Text with button

The same message, with up to three buttons underneath it. Each button has a link and a label of up to 20 characters.

This is the workhorse for link campaigns. The message explains, the button gets tapped, and you get a click you can count. + Add link adds a second and third button — enough for “Shop now / See sizes / Talk to us” without turning the DM into a menu.

Keep the message concise so the action remains easy to find. The editor lets you write up to 1,000 characters; button labels are limited to 20 characters.

Image with button

A product card: image on top, title, optional subtitle, and up to three buttons underneath. The quick Post editor creates one card. For a swipeable carousel of up to ten cards, use Auto DM product link carousel in Templates or the Product carousel node in Flow builder.

See Media in DMs for upload formats and limits.

Attachment

Sends a file — image, video, GIF, audio or PDF — instead of a formatted message. Also in Media in DMs.

Choosing

You want to… Use
Answer a question, sound human Plain text
Send one link and count the taps Text with button
Show a product, or several Image with button
Deliver a guide, price list or clip Attachment

Pro Tip

Switching layout keeps the text you’ve already written where it can carry over, so it’s cheap to try one against another. Watch the live preview on the right as you switch — it helps you review the message before testing it in Instagram.

Text messages can use variations. The quick editor’s attachment and product-card layouts do not rotate uploaded media.

title: Send Images, Video, GIFs and Carousels in a DM
html:
Two of the four message layouts send media rather than text: image with button builds a card, and attachment sends a file.

Image cards and carousels

Pick image with button in a Post automation to create one product card:

  • Product image: upload PNG or JPEG, up to 10 MB. AP3K optimizes the image for delivery.
  • Product title: up to 80 characters.
  • Subtitle: optional, up to 80 characters.
  • Buttons: up to three, each with a destination URL and a label of up to 20 characters.

For multiple cards, choose the Auto DM product link carousel template or the Product carousel node in Flow builder. A carousel holds up to ten cards, with up to three links per card.

A carousel is useful when the reader has a choice to make — products, price tiers or services. For one action, a single card or text with button keeps the decision simple.

Pro tip

Put your most relevant product first and test every destination link before publishing.

Attachments

Pick attachment and you get an upload box: drop a file in, click Upload file, Record audio for a voice note, or Pick recent to reuse something you’ve already sent.

What you can send

Type Formats Limit
Image PNG, JPG, GIF 8 MB
Video MP4, MOV 25 MB
Audio AAC, M4A, WAV 25 MB
Document PDF 25 MB

GIFs go through as images — an 8 MB ceiling, which most short loops fit under comfortably, but a long screen recording exported as a GIF will not. Export it as MP4 instead and it gets the 25 MB video allowance.

Using them well

  • PDFs are delivered as a Download PDF button linking to the saved file. Test the download from another Instagram account.
  • Video works for demos and unboxings, where showing beats describing.
  • Voice notes are unusually effective for high-touch services — a fifteen second “hey, thanks for commenting” in your actual voice reads as personal in a way no text can.

Attachments send on their own

An attachment is the whole message — there’s no caption field alongside it. If the file needs context, add an opener message before it — that one does take text and a button.

Uploads are fixed for the saved attachment or card. Text variations do not swap media files between recipients.

Record audio

  1. Select Record audio and allow microphone access when your browser asks.
  2. Start recording, then stop when your message is ready.
  3. Listen to the recording. Choose Upload to keep it, Re-record to start again, or Discard to remove it.
  4. Wait for the upload to finish before saving or publishing.

Pick recent lists your saved uploads for reuse. If a file fails, check its format and size, then retry before publishing.

title: Message Variations: Stop Every DM Reading the Same
html:
An automation that sends one message sends it perfectly, identically, every time. That’s the problem. A hundred people receiving a character-for-character identical DM is the most legible bot signal there is — to the people reading it, and to the platform delivering it.

Variations are alternate wordings of the same DM. AP3K chooses among your original and saved variations for a conversation. Different people may receive the same variation; a retried delivery keeps the same wording for that journey.

Adding them

The Variations strip sits at the top of the Message card, above the text. Click Add variations — or Edit variations (5) once some exist.

The dialog opens with your message as the starting point and generates alternates from it.

Each variation has its own box, a regenerate icon to rewrite just that one, and a bin to delete it. Regenerate at the top rewrites the whole set. Edit any of them by typing — they’re normal text fields, and the AI’s suggestion is a starting point rather than the finished copy. Save when you’re happy.

How many

Five is the practical target and what the dialog generates by default. Below three, the rotation is noticeable to anyone who compares notes; above five, you’re maintaining copy nobody will read closely.

What to vary

Vary the wrapper, not the payload.

The link, the offer, the discount code and the instruction have to be identical in every variation — that’s the thing you’re actually sending. What changes is the sentence around it:

  • “Here’s the link: …”
  • “Check this out: …”
  • “As promised 👇 …”
  • “Link’s right here: …”
  • “Sending it over now — …”

Keep them the same length and register. A set where one variation is a chirpy two-liner and another is a formal paragraph doesn’t read as natural variety, it reads as two different people.

Check every variation before you publish

Variations rotate without further review, so a typo or a broken link in one variation can reach recipients even when your own test used a different version. Read all of them.

Where else they apply

In the quick editor, variations apply to plain text and text-with-button messages. Your links and buttons stay the same. They do not change attachment files or product-card images.

The same idea drives multiple public replies. The Randomizer node splits people down different flow paths instead of rewording one message.

You can save up to ten alternate messages in addition to the original. Use Write my own to add reviewed copy, or generate more when AI drafting is available.

title: Add a Delay Between Automation Steps
html:
An instant reply is the one thing no human has ever sent. Someone comments, and half a second later a perfectly formatted DM arrives — the timing alone gives it away.

Delay puts a pause between two steps.

Turning delays on

In the Post editor, switch on Enable delay. The Add delay control appears below the trigger. Open it, enter an amount, choose seconds, minutes or hours, then click Add delay to apply it.

Click the saved delay to edit it, or remove it with ×. Switching Enable delay off resets this wait to zero. Save or publish the automation to persist the change.

This is one delivery wait, not a separate delay for every card. For independent waits between multiple steps, use a Delay node in Flow builder. Follow-up messages have their own wait selector.

How long

The Post editor accepts a wait from one second to 23 hours. A short delay of five to fifteen seconds keeps an initial response timely. Use longer waits only when they serve the conversation.

Instagram’s messaging window

A comment’s initial private reply does not by itself open a general follow-up window. The person must interact in the DM conversation. Subsequent automated messages need to remain within the allowed window after their inbound interaction. A delay does not extend that window.

Delivery is scheduled and may occur later than the selected minimum wait. Publishing checks scheduling availability; if the scheduler is not ready, resolve the readiness error before relying on delayed delivery.

Where delays earn their keep

  • Before the initial DM — a short pause while the offer is still relevant.
  • Between flow steps — separate messages with a Delay node.
  • Before a follow-up — choose the follow-up wait and condition together.

Test a short wait from a second account before using a long one in a live campaign.

title: Opener Message: Get a Tap Before You Send the Link
html:
An opener message is a short greeting with a button, sent before the message that actually carries your link.

It looks like a wasted step. It isn’t — it’s the step that gets your link opened.

Why it works

A first DM may appear in message requests. An opener gives the person a clear button to tap before AP3K sends the main content. Their interaction allows the conversation to continue within Instagram’s messaging rules.

It also filters for interest: someone who taps Get the link has chosen to continue. Inbox placement remains controlled by Instagram; an opener does not guarantee placement in the primary inbox.

Setting it up

Click Opener message in the row of add-on buttons. Fill in Opening message (up to 640 characters) and Continue quick reply (up to 20 characters). Use {{username}} where you want the recipient’s handle.

The main message waits until the recipient taps the continuation button. Preview the wording, then test both the initial DM and the button from a second account.

Writing one

Keep it to one or two lines. The opener’s whole job is earning a tap, so anything that isn’t working towards the tap is in the way.

  • Greet them by name. Hey {{username}}! — it makes the greeting specific to the recipient.
  • Say what the button does. “Get the link”, “Send me the guide”, “Show me the code”. Never “Click here” — the label is the promise.
  • Don’t explain the offer yet. That’s the next message’s job.

A working opener:

Hey {{username}}! So glad you commented 😊 Tap below and I’ll send that link straight over.

Pro Tip

Put a delay of five to ten seconds before the opener. An instant greeting the moment someone comments is the tell-tale sign of automation; a few seconds reads as you noticing.

Opener, or ask to follow?

They’re different asks and they stack in this order:

  1. Opener message — get a tap, warm up the thread
  2. Ask to follow — require a follow before the DM goes out
  3. Collect email — ask for contact details
  4. Message — deliver what you promised

Each one adds friction. Adding all four to a giveaway will cost you entrants — pick the ones whose value you’d defend out loud.
description:
An opener message is a short greeting with a button, sent before the message
that actually carries your link.

title: Ask to Follow Before Sending the DM
html:
Ask to follow to receive DM holds the message back until the recipient follows you. It’s the follow-for-value trade, run automatically: they wanted the link, the link costs a follow.

How the follow check works

On a paid plan, add Ask to follow from the buttons under the DM section. In a Post automation, keep the Opener message enabled so the person can start the conversation.

  1. AP3K checks whether the person follows the connected account. People who already follow skip the request.
  2. Other recipients get your follow request and a verification button. They follow the account, then tap the button so AP3K can check again before continuing.

The button does not substitute for following: delivery depends on the follow check. If Instagram cannot confirm the status, do not assume the gate has passed.

Editing the copy

Edit Follow request DM (up to 640 characters) and Verification button (up to 20 characters). These are the two editable fields in the quick editor.

Keep the ask light and explain the value: “Follow our account, then tap below and I’ll send the guide.” The recipient should know what they will receive and how to continue.

When to use it — and when not to

Worth it for giveaways, exclusive drops, and any lead magnet where “follow to enter” was already the deal you announced in the caption.

Not worth it for customer support, order questions, or anything a paying customer asked for. Making someone follow you before you’ll answer their question about a delivery is the fastest way to turn a customer into an ex-one.

It will cost you conversions

Every gate loses people. Some proportion of your commenters will read the ask, decide the link isn’t worth a follow, and leave. That’s the trade — a smaller number of more committed followers. Make sure the thing behind the gate is worth it, and say what it is in the ask.

Ordering it

Ask to follow sits after the opener message and before collecting contact details. One gate is usually plenty — asking for a follow and an email and a phone number before delivering a free checklist is three chances to be told no.

title: Collect an Email or Phone Number in the DM
html:
A DM conversation is a lead you can only reach on one platform. Collect email and Collect phone turn it into one you own — asked for in the thread, validated on the spot, and saved to Contacts.

Both are added from Collect info in the row of step buttons.

Collect email

On a paid plan, choose Collect info → Email. Write the Email request, up to 640 characters. A single clear question usually works best.

AP3K waits for a valid email reply before continuing. An invalid reply is not saved as an email address; the person can retry. The quick editor does not expose a separate custom retry-message field.

Collect phone

Choose Collect info → Phone and write the Phone request, up to 640 characters. Ask for the country code and include an example such as +14155550123.

AP3K validates the reply before saving it to the sender’s contact. Ask for one piece of information per message so the person knows exactly what to send.

Where the answers go

Valid replies save to Contacts, against the Instagram profile that sent them. If someone drops out later, details already captured remain on that contact. Open Contacts to review or export them.

Asking well

  • Give first, ask second. Put the collect step after they’ve received something, or at minimum after the opener. Asking for an email before you’ve delivered anything is a form nobody filled in.
  • Say why. “Where should I send the guide?” outperforms “Enter your email” — the first is a delivery question, the second is a data request.
  • Ask for one thing. Email or phone. Both, back to back, reads as a signup form and gets abandoned like one.
  • Match the channel to the follow-up. Only collect a phone number if you genuinely intend to text or call. Collecting it because the field exists builds a list you’ll never use and a permission you didn’t need.

Consent isn’t implied

Someone answering an email question has not automatically subscribed to a newsletter. Explain your intended use in the request and record the consent your own process requires.

Ordering it

Collect steps come last, after the opener message and any ask to follow, and before the message that delivers what you promised — so the exchange is a fair one: they give you an address, and the thing they wanted arrives right after.

For Post automations, collecting details requires the Opener message. If the person has already messaged you in a Story or Chat automation, the inbound message starts the conversation.

validated on the spot, and saved…

title: Follow-Up Messages and When They Send
html:
Most people who receive your DM won’t act on it the first time. They’re mid-scroll, the link gets read later, later never arrives.

A follow-up message is the second attempt — and because you can attach a condition to it, it goes only to the people who need it.

Adding one

On a paid plan, click Follow up message in the add-on row. Write a text message of up to 640 characters, choose Send when, then set Minimum wait before sending to 15 or 30 minutes, or 1, 3 or 12 hours. The quick follow-up does not have separate attachment or button layouts.

The conditions

Always sends to everyone who reached this point, no condition applied.

Message

  • Seen message — they opened the DM
  • Not seen message — they didn’t
  • Reacted with emoji — they tapped a reaction on it

Link

  • Clicked the link — they tapped through
  • Didn’t click the link — they didn’t

Follow

  • Followed you — they followed after the DM
  • Unfollowed you — they left

Choosing the right one

The condition is what separates a useful nudge from a message people mute you over. Match it to what you actually want to happen next.

Not seen message is the safest and usually the most valuable. These people never saw the first DM at all — very often it’s sitting in message requests. A follow-up here isn’t a repeat, it’s a first delivery.

Didn’t click the link is the conversion nudge. They read it and didn’t act, so the second message should give a different reason rather than repeat the first — a deadline, an objection answered, a shorter ask.

Clicked the link is the one people forget, and it’s the warmest audience you have. They’re interested. Follow up with the next step: a question, a discount, a booking link.

Reacted with emoji is a reply without words. A 🔥 on a product DM is permission to keep talking.

Followed you pairs naturally with ask to follow — thank them, or deliver the thing the follow unlocked.

Unfollowed you should almost always be left alone. Someone who just left is telling you they want fewer messages, and a follow-up argues with that.

Time it inside 24 hours

A follow-up requires an inbound DM interaction and must remain within the allowed messaging window. In Post automations, enable the Opener message and wait for the recipient to tap. A comment alone does not authorize an unrestricted sequence. If the window closes before the scheduled job runs, the follow-up is not sent.

Writing one

  • Don’t resend the first message. They either didn’t see it or weren’t convinced, and a copy fixes neither.
  • Keep it shorter than the first. One line and the link.
  • Give an out. “If it’s not for you, no worries at all” costs you nothing and stops the nudge reading as pressure.
  • One follow-up. Two is persistence, three is the block button.

A follow-up on Not seen message:

Hey — think this landed in your requests 👀 Here’s that link again in case it got buried.

Delivery and receipts

Conditions are checked after the wait. Seen and reaction conditions depend on Instagram receipts. Followed and Unfollowed require confirmed before-and-after follow status. A newer inbound reply can cancel an outdated reminder, and a paused automation or closed messaging window can stop delivery.

Test with a short supported wait and the Always condition first. Then test the condition your campaign actually needs. Scheduler availability and Instagram delivery rules still apply.

the link gets read later, later never arrives.

title: Automation Settings: Run the Public Reply Without the DM
html:
The ⋯ button at the top right of the Setup direct message section holds the settings for the DM half of the automation.

Disable direct message

One toggle, with a consequence worth reading twice: when disabled, only the public comment reply works.

Switch it on and the automation still watches the post, still matches your trigger, and still replies publicly under the comment. It just doesn’t send anything to anyone’s inbox. Everything you built in the DM section — the opener, the collect steps, the message, the follow-up — stays saved exactly as it is, and comes back the moment you switch it off.

When to use it

Comment engagement without the DM load. Some posts want a lively comment section and nothing more. A public reply to every comment is engagement Instagram can see; a DM to every commenter is send volume you may not want to spend.

Testing your triggers safely. Publish with DMs disabled, comment from a second account, and confirm the right keywords fire and the public replies read well — without a single real person receiving a half-finished DM.

Pausing a campaign mid-flight. The offer sold out, the link broke, the code expired. Disabling the DM stops delivery immediately while the automation stays live and your comment section keeps answering. It’s a far lighter action than unpublishing, and nothing has to be rebuilt to resume.

A post that outgrew its automation. Something went unexpectedly viral and the DM volume is more than you want. Turn off the DM, keep the replies.

The public reply is now the whole message

With DMs off, the reply under the comment is all anyone gets — so “check your DMs!” becomes a promise the automation no longer keeps. Rewrite your public replies to stand on their own before you disable the DM, or people will go looking for a message that isn’t coming.

What it doesn’t do

This setting applies to the automation you are editing. It does not pause other automations, and it cannot retract a DM Instagram has already received. Save or publish the change, then test that new matching comments receive only the intended public reply.

title: Post Automation Templates
html:
Building a post automation from scratch means deciding the trigger, the reply, the DM layout and the follow-up before you’ve seen one working. The template gallery skips that: nine ready-made post automations, each already wired for one common job, waiting for your post and your copy.

Opening the gallery

Click New automation, then Browse templates. Filter by All, Basic or Flow, or search by the job you want to do. Some Basic templates use a flow underneath to support multi-step behavior; review the editor they open.

The gallery has 16 templates: 13 under Basic and three under Flow. Cards show the automation type and whether a paid plan is required.

The nine post templates

Template What it does Built on
Auto-DM from comments
Popular		 DMs anyone who comments on a post or reel Comment-to-DM
Grow followers from comments
Popular		 Asks the commenter to follow you before it sends the content Ask to follow
Auto-DM on all posts and reels One automation covering every post and reel on the account Post selection
Auto-DM on next post or reel Arms itself and waits for your next upload to publish Post selection
Collect email/phone from comments Asks for an email or phone number before it hands over the content Collect email and phone
Auto-DM when someone shares your Post or Reel Replies when someone shares a post or reel into your business inbox Share triggers
Re-engage with follow-up message Sends a second message on conditions and time delays to people who went quiet Follow-ups
Auto-DM from comments with an opener message Sends a short greeting with a button first, then the real content on the tap Opener message
Auto DM product link carousel Sends up to ten clickable links in a single swipeable message Carousels

Which one to start with

Auto-DM from comments is the baseline. Everything else on the list is that automation with one thing added, so it’s the one to open if you want to understand the editor rather than just ship something.

Pick a more specific template when the shape of the campaign is already decided:

  • Running the same offer across your whole feed → Auto-DM on all posts and reels
  • Launching something tomorrow → Auto-DM on next post or reel, set up before you upload
  • Building a mailing list, not just clicks → Collect email/phone from comments
  • Growing the account rather than the list → Grow followers from comments
  • Sending several links at once → Auto DM product link carousel

The opener template is worth a look

Auto-DM from comments with an opener message gets the recipient to tap a continuation button before the main content arrives. That interaction lets AP3K continue the conversation within Instagram’s messaging rules; it does not guarantee primary-inbox placement.

Making a template yours

A template opens as an unpublished draft with a placeholder name and a Draft badge, so nothing goes out while you edit. Work down the editor:

1. Point it at a post. The Post card is the one thing no template can guess. Templates that say all posts or next post have already made this choice for you — check it’s the one you wanted.

2. Set the trigger words. Replace generic keywords with the word in your caption. For a quick Post automation, choose Any comment or a specific word (s). Flow templates expose their own trigger settings.

3. Rewrite the message. Placeholder copy reads like placeholder copy. Replace it, put your real link in, and use {{username}} where a name belongs. Then add variations so a hundred people don’t all receive the identical message.

4. Check the steps the template added. An opener, a collect-info step or a follow-up arrives pre-wired with its own copy and conditions — read those too, not just the main message.

5. Publish, then test from a second account. Comment your own keyword and watch the DM arrive. It’s the only check that covers the whole chain.

Templates are also worth reading

Opening a template close to what you want and looking at how it’s assembled is the fastest way to learn the editor — which steps were added, in what order, and what each one is for. You can close it without publishing.

title: Create an Instagram Story Automation
html:
A story automation replies to the people who react to your story, answer it with a message, or tag you in a story of their own. These interactions arrive through Instagram messaging, so the automation answers the person in a DM.

Before you begin

  • An Instagram professional account connected to AP3K.
  • A second account for testing the story interaction.
  • The message or resource you want to send.

Start a story automation

Choose New automation → Story automation. The editor opens with Setup Triggers and Setup Direct Message. There is no public comment reply because the event is a story interaction.

1. Choose the story interaction

Open Story interaction and select the event that should start the automation:

OptionWhen it fires
Mentions meSomeone tags the connected account in their story.
ReactsSomeone sends an emoji reaction to your story.
RepliesSomeone sends a text reply to your story.

The quick Story editor selects an interaction type. It does not have a specific-story grid, a next-story selector, keyword filtering or Intent Match. Review the rule summary below the control before publishing.

2. Write the DM

In Message, choose plain text, text with button, or attachment. Text supports up to 1,000 characters; link messages can have up to three buttons. Use {{username}} to personalize the message and review the phone preview.

Add variations helps create alternate wordings for text messages. Review every variation and keep the link and offer consistent.

3. Add optional steps

Paid plans can add Collect info, Ask to follow and Follow up message. These can capture an email or phone number, check follow status, or send a conditional reminder. Story interactions already start in DMs, so the quick Story editor has no separate Opener message step.

The AP3K AI reply message option uses your AI knowledge, behavior and guardrails on a paid plan. Choose a saved message instead if you need collection or follow-up steps in the same quick automation.

4. Publish and test

Name the automation and click Publish. From another account, perform the exact interaction you selected: mention, reaction or text reply. Check the DM, every button and any capture step.

Messaging window

Story replies are inbound conversations. Follow-ups must stay within Instagram’s allowed messaging window; scheduling a wait does not keep a conversation open indefinitely.

You should now have a tested Story automation for the interaction you chose. Next: Story automation templates.

title: Story Automation Templates
html:
The Basic template gallery includes Respond to story mentions. Open it from New automation → Browse templates, then choose Basic or search for “story”.

Respond to story mentions

Send a thank-you message, offer or link when someone mentions you in their story. Someone tagging your account is already opening a conversation; the template gives you a starting response.

What it arrives with

  • A Story automation using Mentions me.
  • A saved thank-you DM to customize.
  • The same message and optional engagement controls as the quick Story editor.

What to change before publishing

Rewrite the message. A thank-you can include a discount code, the resource they mentioned, or a question that keeps the thread going. Replace placeholders with your real offer.

Review variations. If you add alternate copy, make sure every version still promises the same thing. Use {{username}} where a handle fits naturally.

Check the next step. A paid plan can collect contact details or add a follow-up, but only add a question when its purpose is clear.

Test a real mention

Instagram only sends the events and media your connected account is allowed to access. Visibility and privacy settings can affect a mention. Test from another account and check the connection if a particular event is missing.

Other story interactions

For an emoji reaction or text reply, create a new Story automation and choose Reacts or Replies. The quick editor watches the interaction type rather than selecting one story from a grid.

title: How Chat Automation Works
html:
AP3K has three quick automation types, distinguished by where the person is when they trigger one:

AutomationFires when someone…
Post automationComments on the selected post or reel.
Story automationPerforms the selected story interaction.
Chat automationSends a matching message to your inbox.

A Chat automation has no post or story attached. It watches incoming DMs and responds when its keyword rule matches.

What a Chat automation contains

  • Trigger: specific keywords or Any incoming DM.
  • Message: plain text, text with button, attachment, or a paid AP3K AI reply.
  • Optional paid steps: Collect info, Ask to follow and Follow up message for saved-message automations.

The editor uses cards and a phone preview. For a branching conversation with choices, custom fields and multiple messages, use Flow builder or a lead-capture template.

When to use one

Chat automation answers a call to action such as “DM me BOOK”. It works for bio instructions, a welcome response, resource delivery or common questions. Choose a Post automation when the trigger is a public comment.

Keep a quick Chat automation for a focused response. Reach for the Flow builder when the next message depends on which choice a person taps, a stored answer, a tag or a condition.

What is different from Post automation

  • No public comment reply: there is no comment to answer.
  • No post picker: the incoming message is the event.
  • No separate opener: the person has already messaged you.

The messaging window is already running

The inbound DM starts a conversation. Automated replies and follow-ups must remain within Instagram’s allowed window after the person’s latest interaction.

Ready to build one? Create a Chat automation.

title: Create an Instagram Chat Automation
html:
A Chat automation answers people who message your inbox directly — the “DM me BOOK” call to action. This guide takes you from an empty automation to a tested response.

Before you begin

  • An Instagram account connected to AP3K.
  • A second Instagram account to test from.
  • Your campaign keyword and the response it should send.

Open the Chat editor

Choose New automation → Chat automation. Rename the automation so it is easy to identify later. The editor shows the trigger above your message and a conversation preview alongside it.

1. Set the trigger keywords

Choose a specific word (s). Type one keyword into Add keyword and press Enter, or use the plus button. Repeat for alternatives such as pricing, price and cost. Remove a keyword with its ×.

Keywords match without case sensitivity inside incoming messages. Choose deliberate campaign words: BOOK is more focused than a common greeting.

Choose Any incoming DM only when every eligible message should receive this response. That option ignores the keyword list. Check other active automations to avoid overlapping replies.

2. Write the message

Open Message and choose plain text, text with button or attachment. Text supports up to 1,000 characters. For buttons, complete each label and destination URL; you can add up to three.

Write the opening of a conversation, not a broadcast. Review the preview and use Add variations if you want alternate approved wordings.

3. Add conversation steps

Paid plans can add Collect info, Ask to follow and Follow up message to a saved-message automation. A collected email or phone is stored on the contact who sent it.

For branching choices, a multi-question script or a custom answer field, open Flow builder instead. See Choices and collecting replies.

The paid AP3K AI reply option uses the person’s message plus your AI knowledge and guardrails. Configure a safe fallback message. AI reply mode cannot be combined with the quick editor’s capture and follow-up steps.

4. Publish and test

Click Publish, then send the keyword from your second account. Confirm the response, link destinations and any capture behavior.

Test the wrong input too: send a message without the keyword and confirm the campaign does not trigger. Then send a sentence containing the keyword and confirm the expected match. If you chose Any incoming DM, test that broader rule deliberately.

You should now have a tested Chat automation. For more complex conversations, continue with Chat automation templates.
description: A Chat automation answers people who message your inbox directly — the “DM me BOOK” call to action. This guide takes you from an empty automation to a tested response.

title: Chat Choices, Branches and Collecting Replies
html:
Choices let a person pick a direction. Capture steps let the automation wait for something they type and save it to their contact. In AP3K, use the quick Chat editor for a saved response and email or phone collection; use Flow builder for branching choices and custom answers.

Adding choices in Flow builder

Add a question/choice step, write the question and give each choice a short label. Connect each option to the message or step that should follow it. A choice should lead somewhere useful before you publish.

For example, “What are you here for?” can offer Get expert tips and Discover products. Each option leads to its own response. A link button opens a website; a choice routes the conversation. Use the right kind of button for the job.

Keep the labels short. Two or three words are easier to read in a chat bubble than a full sentence. Use a Condition node when the branch depends on stored information instead of a button tap.

Collecting a reply

In a quick Chat automation, choose Collect info → Email or Phone on a paid plan. Write the request. The automation waits for the reply, validates it and saves a valid value to the sender’s contact.

In Flow builder, use an email, phone or capture-answer step. Set the next connection so the conversation continues after the answer. Capture-answer stores free text in the field you select.

Email, phone and free text

TypeUse it for
EmailA valid email address.
PhoneA phone number; ask for the country code.
Capture answerA name, city or other free-text value in a flow field.

Email and phone details appear in Contacts on the profile that provided them. Free text needs a clear question because the automation cannot infer whether an arbitrary answer is useful.

Ask for one thing at a time

Every question is a point where someone may stop replying. Ask only for details the next step needs, explain why, and confirm what happens after the person answers.

A worked conversation

  1. Greet and offer choices: “What are you here for?”
  2. Branch: each choice leads to a response that answers it.
  3. Collect where useful: request an email in the branch that needs one.
  4. Confirm: deliver the promised link or explain the next step.

The Capture leads from DMs and Sell products or services from DMs templates demonstrate these flow patterns.

title: Chat Automation Templates
html:
The Basic template gallery includes three inbox-focused starting points: answer a message, collect details, or offer a choice of products and services. Open New automation → Browse templates and select Basic or search for “DM”.

Respond to all your DMs

One trigger, one welcome message. This is the simplest starting point for the quick Chat editor.

What it arrives with: a greeting keyword such as Hello and a saved welcome response.

What to change: replace the keyword with the one in your bio or caption. If you really want to answer all incoming messages, choose Any incoming DM. Rewrite the message with a useful next action or a button link.

Capture leads from DMs

This paid template uses a flow to collect an email, phone number and name before a confirmation. The starting keyword is connect.

What to change: remove any question you do not need, explain what the person gets and review the connections between steps. Email and phone values are saved to the sender’s contact; the name step captures a free-text answer.

Three questions in a row can feel like a form. If you only need an email for the requested guide, keep the conversation focused on that.

Sell products or services from DMs

This paid flow template starts with Hello, asks how it can help and offers Get expert tips or Discover products.

What to change: rename the choices to your actual categories, write each branch and replace every placeholder URL. Test every branch; the first message is only the beginning of the conversation.

Make a template yours

  1. Give it a clear campaign name.
  2. Set the keyword or incoming-message rule.
  3. Replace placeholder copy and links.
  4. Review any paid features and the next-step connections.
  5. Publish, then test from a second account.

You can also build a Chat automation from scratch, or learn more about choices and collecting replies.
